questions.q: What type of party system does the U.S. have?
questions.correct: Two-party system
incorrect: Single-party system
Multi-party system
Non-partisan system
questions.why_correct: Nearly all U.S. elections are contested between Democrats and Republicans.
why_wrong: A single-party system allows only one party — the U.S. has free, competitive elections.
Multi-party systems have many parties regularly winning power — third parties rarely win major U.S. offices.
The U.S. officially recognizes parties and organizes primaries by party.
questions.tip: Think about every presidential election — which two parties always have the candidates?

questions.q: What does it mean to be a CONSERVATIVE?
questions.correct: Favoring traditional values, limited government, and free markets
incorrect: Favoring expanded programs, social equality, and progressive change
Believing government should have no role in society at all
Supporting government ownership of major businesses and industries
questions.why_correct: Conservatives want to preserve traditional institutions, limit government size, and let the market operate with minimal regulation.
why_wrong: Expanded programs and progressive change describe a liberal viewpoint.
Rejecting all government involvement describes libertarianism — conservatives still support some government roles.
Government ownership of industry is socialism — conservatives favor private ownership.
questions.tip: 'Conserve' means to keep. Conservatives want to keep traditional values and limit change.

questions.q: What does it mean to be a LIBERAL?
questions.correct: Favoring government action to promote social equality and opportunity
incorrect: Favoring limited government and traditional social values instead
Believing government should never regulate the economy or society
Wanting to replace democracy with a different form of government
questions.why_correct: Liberals support using government programs to reduce inequality and expand opportunity.
why_wrong: Limited government and traditional values describe a conservative.
Opposing all regulation describes libertarianism — liberals support regulation to protect people.
Liberalism works within the democratic system — it does not seek to replace government.
questions.tip: Liberals focus on expanding freedoms and opportunities for all through government action.

questions.correct: Any party other than the Democratic or Republican parties
incorrect: A breakaway faction inside the Republican Party
A party that controls one chamber but not the other
A temporary alliance formed between the two major parties
questions.why_correct: Third parties — like the Green, Libertarian, or historic Bull Moose Party — are any parties outside the two dominant ones.
why_wrong: A third party is a separate, independent party — not an internal faction.
Control of chambers does not define a third party.
A temporary alliance is a coalition — not a third party.
questions.tip: If there are already two main parties, what would you call any other competing party?

questions.correct: One specific policy position on a single issue
incorrect: The full collection of all the party's positions
The party's official name and visual branding
The complete list of candidates the party nominated
questions.why_correct: A plank is one specific policy stance — e.g., 'support Medicare for all.' Many planks together form the platform.
why_wrong: The full collection of all positions is the platform — a plank is just one piece.
Name and branding are the party's identity — not a policy position.
Nominated candidates are the party's ticket — not a plank.
questions.tip: A platform is built from individual planks. Which is the whole, and which is just one part?

questions.correct: The complete set of all the party's policy positions
incorrect: A single specific position on one policy issue
The physical stage where party candidates give speeches
The party's official strategy for raising campaign funds
questions.why_correct: The platform covers all major issues — economy, healthcare, foreign policy — and tells voters what the party stands for.
why_wrong: A single policy position is a plank — the platform is the full collection.
The physical stage is a podium — a platform is a document of policy positions.
Fundraising strategy is a campaign operation, not the platform.
questions.tip: A platform is what a party STANDS on. Individual pieces of it (single issues) are called planks.

questions.correct: Parties moving toward extremes, making compromise harder
incorrect: An equal division of seats between parties in Congress
The process of redrawing congressional district boundaries
A formal alliance formed between two political parties
questions.why_correct: Polarization means Democrats move further left and Republicans further right, reducing common ground.
why_wrong: An equal seat split describes a divided Congress — polarization is about ideological distance.
Redrawing districts is gerrymandering — related to elections but not polarization.
A formal alliance is a coalition — polarization is increased division, not alliance.
questions.tip: Think of a magnet's poles pulling apart — polarization means the two sides keep moving farther away.

questions.q: Which is a role of political parties?
questions.correct: Recruiting candidates and linking voters to elected officials
incorrect: Writing, passing, and enforcing all government laws
Appointing federal judges and approving the cabinet
Setting interest rates and managing the money supply
questions.why_correct: Parties bridge citizens and government — they select candidates, mobilize voters, and coordinate government.
why_wrong: Laws are written by Congress and enforced by the executive branch.
Judges are appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
Interest rates and money supply are controlled by the Federal Reserve.
questions.tip: Think of parties as organizers and connectors between voters and the people who run government.

questions.correct: A local party meeting where members vote for preferred candidates
incorrect: A secret ballot election that is open to all voters
A televised debate held between the presidential candidates
A closed party meeting where leaders quietly pick the nominee
questions.why_correct: In a caucus, voters meet in person, discuss candidates, and indicate their preference — unlike a private primary ballot.
why_wrong: A secret ballot open to all voters describes a primary — not a caucus.
A televised debate is a campaign event, not a caucus.
In a caucus, regular members vote — it's not limited to leaders picking in secret.
questions.tip: A caucus is a meeting where people show up together. How is that different from casting a secret ballot alone?

questions.correct: A ballot cast by mail when a voter can't be present on Election Day
incorrect: A ballot thrown out because the voter forgot to sign it
A ballot used by voters who missed the registration deadline
A temporary ballot given when registration can't be confirmed
questions.why_correct: Absentee ballots let voters who are traveling or ill participate by mailing in their vote before Election Day.
why_wrong: An unsigned ballot may be rejected, but that's not what absentee means.
Missing the registration deadline means you generally can't vote — absentee is for registered voters.
A ballot for unconfirmed registrations is a provisional ballot — different from absentee.
questions.tip: 'Absent' means not present. An absentee ballot lets you vote when you can't appear in person.

questions.correct: The smallest local geographic unit for organizing elections
incorrect: The national headquarters building of a political party
A large congressional district covering multiple counties
The official deadline window for returning absentee ballots
questions.why_correct: A precinct is a neighborhood-level unit — voters are assigned to one based on their address, and it has its own polling place.
why_wrong: National party HQ is a centralized office — a precinct is a small local area.
A congressional district is much larger and contains many precincts.
A ballot deadline is an election rule — not a geographic unit.
questions.tip: A precinct is the smallest piece of the election map — your local voting neighborhood.

questions.correct: Citizens propose a new law by collecting enough voter signatures
incorrect: Voters remove an elected official before the term ends
Voters approve or reject a law passed by the legislature
A party formally announces its goals and policy positions
questions.why_correct: Through an initiative, citizens bypass the legislature — they write a law, gather signatures, and put it on the ballot.
why_wrong: Voters removing an official is a recall — not an initiative.
Voters approving a legislative law is a referendum — not an initiative.
A party's formal goals are its platform — not an initiative.
questions.tip: An initiative lets citizens take the initiative — they start the process of creating a law.

questions.correct: Voters directly approve or reject a specific law or measure
incorrect: Citizens propose a new law by gathering voter signatures
Voters remove an elected official before the term ends
Voters choose a party's nominee in a preliminary election
questions.why_correct: In a referendum, voters decide directly on a measure — often a law from the legislature sent to the public for approval.
why_wrong: Citizens proposing laws through signatures is an initiative.
Removing an official is a recall.
Choosing a party's nominee is a primary.
questions.tip: A referendum refers a question to the voters — the proposal usually comes from the government.

questions.correct: Voters remove an elected official before the term ends
incorrect: Citizens propose a new law by collecting signatures
Voters approve or reject a law passed by the legislature
A disputed election is repeated to confirm the results
questions.why_correct: Citizens gather signatures to put the question on the ballot, then voters decide whether to remove the official.
why_wrong: Citizens proposing a new law through signatures is an initiative.
Voters approving a legislative law is a referendum.
Repeating a disputed election is a revote — not a recall.
questions.tip: 'Recall' means to call back. A recall election calls an official back out of office.

questions.q: What is a STRAIGHT TICKET vote?
questions.correct: Voting for every candidate from the same party
incorrect: Voting for candidates from more than one party
Voting early rather than on Election Day itself
Voting only for the top of the ballot (president or governor)
questions.why_correct: A straight-ticket voter selects the same party's candidate for every office on the ballot.
why_wrong: Choosing candidates from more than one party is a split ticket.
When you vote has nothing to do with straight vs. split ticket.
Voting only for top offices is an incomplete ballot — not a straight ticket.
questions.tip: Straight = same party all the way down. Split = mixing parties for different offices.

questions.correct: Only registered party members may vote in that party's primary
incorrect: Any registered voter may vote in any party's primary
The primary is conducted entirely through mail-in ballots
The primary is canceled when only one candidate files to run
questions.why_correct: In a closed primary, you must be a registered Democrat to vote in the Democratic primary — independents can't participate.
why_wrong: Any voter choosing any party's primary describes an open primary.
Voting method is unrelated to the open/closed distinction.
Closed refers to who is eligible to vote — not whether there's competition.
questions.tip: Closed = restricted to party members only. Which type leaves out independent voters?

questions.correct: Any registered voter may vote regardless of party affiliation
incorrect: Only registered party members may vote in that party's primary
The primary ballot is open for viewing by the general public
Primary results are announced publicly as soon as polls close
questions.why_correct: In an open primary, voters don't need a party registration — anyone can choose which party's primary to vote in.
why_wrong: Only party members voting describes a closed primary.
'Open' refers to voter eligibility — not ballot transparency.
Announcing results is standard election procedure — not what defines an open primary.
questions.tip: Open = open to everyone. Which type lets independent voters participate?

questions.correct: Voters directly choose their party's nominee for the general election
incorrect: Party leaders meet privately and choose the nominee themselves
The primary stage is skipped and candidates go straight to general
Only voters who donated to the party may participate in choosing
questions.why_correct: A direct primary puts nominee selection in voters' hands — now the standard method in U.S. elections.
why_wrong: Party leaders choosing the nominee without voters is a brokered or convention system.
A direct primary is still a primary — 'direct' means voters choose, not that it's skipped.
Donation requirements for voting do not exist and are unconstitutional.
questions.tip: Direct = voters decide directly. Who makes the final choice of the nominee in a direct primary?

questions.correct: The final election where voters choose between party nominees for office
incorrect: A preliminary election where parties narrow down their candidates
An election held specifically for congressional seats only
A local election covering only a single city or county district
questions.why_correct: The general election — held in November — is the main contest where the winner takes office.
why_wrong: Narrowing candidates within a party is a primary — the general comes after.
General elections include presidential and state races — not just Congress.
General elections are held at all levels — federal, state, and local.
questions.tip: Primary → General. The primary picks one nominee per party. The general is the final contest.

questions.q: How many Electoral College votes are needed to win the presidency?
questions.correct: 270 out of 538 total electoral votes
incorrect: A simple majority of the national popular vote
300 or more out of 538 total electoral votes
Two-thirds of all 538 electoral votes (about 359)
questions.why_correct: There are 538 total electoral votes. A candidate needs a majority — 270 — to win outright.
why_wrong: Winning the popular vote doesn't guarantee the presidency — Al Gore won it in 2000 but lost the Electoral College.
300 is not the threshold — 270 is the majority of 538.
Two-thirds is a supermajority — only a simple majority (270) is required.
questions.tip: 538 total votes. You need one more than half. What is half of 538?

questions.q: What is a PLURALITY of votes?
questions.correct: Getting more votes than any other candidate, even without 50%
incorrect: Getting more than 50% of all the votes that were cast
Getting votes from supporters in both major political parties
Getting more electoral votes than any other candidate
questions.why_correct: A plurality means the most votes — even 35% wins if opponents each get less.
why_wrong: More than 50% is a majority — a plurality only requires more than any single opponent.
Support from both parties describes bipartisan appeal — not a plurality.
Electoral votes apply to the presidential race — plurality refers to raw vote totals.
questions.tip: Majority = more than half. Plurality = just the most. Which is easier with many candidates?

questions.correct: Vague positive words like 'freedom' that sound good but mean nothing specific
incorrect: Connecting a candidate to a beloved national symbol or figure
Claiming that everyone is already supporting a candidate
Insulting an opponent with a negative label or name
questions.why_correct: Glittering generalities use virtuous-sounding words that appeal to emotions without making any concrete claim.
why_wrong: Connecting a candidate to a respected symbol is transfer propaganda.
Claiming everyone supports something is bandwagon propaganda.
Insulting with a negative label is name-calling propaganda.
questions.tip: Glittering generalities sound great but say nothing specific. What do 'freedom' and 'family values' actually promise?

questions.correct: Pressuring people to agree because 'everyone else is doing it'
incorrect: Using vague emotional words that appeal to shared values
Showing only the evidence that favors your side
Connecting a candidate to a trusted person or symbol
questions.why_correct: Bandwagon exploits the desire to belong — 'everyone is already on board' — pressuring conformity without giving facts.
why_wrong: Vague emotional words that appeal to values are glittering generalities.
Showing only favorable evidence is stacked cards.
Connecting to a trusted person or symbol is testimonial or transfer propaganda.
questions.tip: 'Jump on the bandwagon' means join the winning side. How does that pressure someone without using facts?

questions.correct: Acting like an ordinary person to seem relatable to average voters
incorrect: Calling an opponent an out-of-touch elite who doesn't care
Using complex language to appear smarter than the opponent
Featuring a celebrity to make the candidate seem glamorous
questions.why_correct: Just-plain-folks shows a candidate eating at diners or talking about humble roots — the goal is to seem trustworthy and relatable.
why_wrong: Calling an opponent out-of-touch is name-calling — this technique is about the candidate's own image.
Complex language would make a candidate seem less accessible — the opposite of this technique.
Celebrity glamour is testimonial or transfer propaganda.
questions.tip: Politicians sometimes wear hard hats or visit farms. What impression are they trying to create?

questions.correct: Showing only the facts that favor your side and hiding the rest
incorrect: Claiming that everyone is already supporting your candidate
Using a respected symbol to make a candidate look patriotic
Using vague positive words with no specific real meaning
questions.why_correct: Card stacking selects only favorable evidence and hides anything that contradicts the message.
why_wrong: Claiming everyone supports something is bandwagon propaganda.
Using respected symbols is transfer propaganda.
Vague positive words with no meaning are glittering generalities.
questions.tip: Stacking the deck means rigging it in your favor. In propaganda, what gets left out?

questions.correct: Labeling someone with a negative term instead of arguing the facts
incorrect: Overstating a candidate's achievements to make them look better
Using vague positive language to make a candidate seem virtuous
Hiding unfavorable facts while highlighting only the good ones
questions.why_correct: Name-calling targets emotions — labels like 'radical' or 'elitist' bypass real argument and persuade through negative association.
why_wrong: Overstating achievements is puffery or plain-folks — name-calling attacks with labels.
Vague positive language is glittering generalities — name-calling uses negative labels.
Hiding unfavorable facts is stacked cards — name-calling attacks directly.
questions.tip: Name-calling skips the argument and goes straight to insults. Why is that persuasive to some people?

questions.q: What is HARD MONEY in campaign finance?
questions.correct: Donations given directly to a candidate's campaign, subject to federal limits
incorrect: Donations given to parties or outside groups with fewer restrictions
Large cash donations made secretly without any public disclosure
Donations of goods or services rather than actual money
questions.why_correct: Hard money goes directly to a candidate and is tightly regulated — there are legal limits on how much individuals and groups can give.
why_wrong: Donations to parties and outside groups with fewer restrictions describes soft money.
All campaign donations must be disclosed — secret donations are illegal.
Donations of goods or services are in-kind contributions — not the hard/soft distinction.
questions.tip: Hard = hard rules, strict limits. Soft = softer rules, fewer limits. Which goes directly to the candidate?

questions.q: What is a SPECIAL INTEREST GROUP?
questions.correct: An organized group that works to influence government on shared goals
incorrect: Voters who consistently support one political party every election
A congressional committee that oversees a specific policy area
A branch of a major party that focuses on a single issue
questions.why_correct: Groups like the NRA, AARP, or Sierra Club organize around shared interests and use lobbying and donations to push for preferred policies.
why_wrong: Voters who always support one party are a party's base — not an interest group.
A congressional committee is a government body — not an outside interest group.
Interest groups are independent organizations — not branches of a party.
questions.tip: Special interest groups represent a specific interest. How do they use that to influence government?

questions.correct: Try to influence lawmakers on behalf of an interest group
incorrect: Run voter registration drives for their preferred political party
Investigate and report on corruption for news organizations
Manage the day-to-day staff operations of Congress members
questions.why_correct: Lobbyists meet with lawmakers, provide research and arguments, and use influence to shape legislation for their clients.
why_wrong: Voter registration drives are run by campaigns and nonprofits — not lobbyists.
Investigating corruption is journalism — not lobbying.
Congressional staff manage day-to-day operations — not lobbyists.
questions.tip: Named for waiting in the lobby of legislatures — what is a lobbyist's main job once inside?

questions.q: What is a Political Action Committee (PAC)?
questions.correct: An organization that raises money to elect or defeat candidates
incorrect: A government agency that investigates campaign finance violations
A party committee that officially selects the party's nominees
A citizen group that organizes protests and public demonstrations
questions.why_correct: PACs — often tied to corporations, unions, or interest groups — collect and spend money to support or oppose candidates.
why_wrong: The FEC investigates campaign finance violations — a PAC is not a government agency.
Nominees are selected through primaries and conventions — not PACs.
Protest organizers may be advocacy groups — a PAC focuses on campaign spending.
questions.tip: PAC = Political Action Committee. Their action is spending money to influence who gets elected.

questions.q: What are the basic qualifications to vote in the U.S.?
questions.correct: U.S. citizen, at least 18 years old, and registered to vote
incorrect: Must own property and have paid federal income taxes
Must pass a literacy test and pay a voting fee
Must hold a college degree and a government-issued passport
questions.why_correct: The three core federal requirements are citizenship, age 18+, and registration. Property and education tests are unconstitutional.
why_wrong: Property and tax requirements were used historically but are now unconstitutional.
Literacy tests and poll taxes were banned by the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Education and passport requirements do not exist — voting is a right of citizenship.
questions.tip: What barriers to voting have been removed over U.S. history? What requirements actually remain today?

questions.q: How have voting rights expanded over U.S. history?
questions.correct: Key amendments extended voting to Black Americans, women, and 18-year-olds
incorrect: Voting rights have gradually narrowed due to stricter ID laws
Voting rights have remained the same since the Constitution was ratified
Federal laws — but no constitutional amendments — changed voting rights
questions.why_correct: The 15th (1870), 19th (1920), 24th (1964), and 26th (1971) Amendments each expanded access.
why_wrong: The overall arc over 200 years has been expansion — not narrowing.
Originally only white male property owners could vote — rights changed dramatically.
Constitutional amendments were the critical tools for expanding voting rights.
questions.tip: Who could vote when the Constitution was written? Which amendments changed that over time?

questions.q: What is the purpose of a NATIONAL CONVENTION?
questions.correct: To officially nominate the party's presidential ticket and adopt its platform
incorrect: To cast the final votes that officially determine the election winner
To formally swear in the newly elected president and vice president
To select the delegates who will later vote in the state primaries
questions.why_correct: Delegates gather to officially nominate the presidential and vice-presidential candidates and approve the party's platform.
why_wrong: The final votes that determine the winner are cast by the Electoral College.
Swearing in the president is the inauguration, held in January.
Delegates are selected before the convention — through primaries and caucuses.
questions.tip: The convention comes after primaries and before the general election. What is its main job?

questions.correct: A survey measuring what the public thinks about candidates or issues
incorrect: A survey taken outside polling places right after people vote
A survey using loaded questions to push people toward one view
An official government count of all eligible registered voters
questions.why_correct: Opinion polls sample the population to gauge their views — the goal is to measure, not change, public opinion.
why_wrong: A survey taken as voters leave polling places is an exit poll.
A survey designed to change opinions through loaded questions is a push poll.
Counting registered voters is a government function — not a poll.
questions.tip: Opinion polls measure what people think. Which type of poll tries to change what people think?

questions.correct: A survey taken outside polling places asking how people just voted
incorrect: A survey asking registered voters why they decided not to vote
A poll that plants negative information to shift voter opinions
A mail survey sent to voters before Election Day to predict results
questions.why_correct: Exit polls are taken as voters leave — news organizations use results to project winners before official counts are in.
why_wrong: Asking non-voters why they didn't vote is a non-voter survey — not an exit poll.
Planting negative information to shift opinions is a push poll.
Mail surveys sent before Election Day are pre-election opinion polls.
questions.tip: Exit polls happen at the exit — after people vote. Why are they more reliable than pre-election polls?

questions.correct: A poll using misleading questions to push people toward one opinion
incorrect: A poll that honestly measures what voters currently think
A poll taken outside polling places right after people vote
A poll conducted by the government to check voter registration
questions.why_correct: A push poll is a campaign tactic disguised as a poll — loaded questions plant negative information about an opponent to shift opinion.
why_wrong: Honestly measuring voter opinion is an opinion poll — push polls try to change opinion.
Polling voters right after they vote is an exit poll.
Checking voter registration is an administrative function — not a poll.
questions.tip: A push poll 'pushes' you toward a conclusion. How is that different from a real poll?
